rewritten_text:
“Joseph!! Joseph!!!” Then he shook his head and tapped it, indicating his opinion of Joseph’s mental shortcomings.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry, you must be exhausted. Sit down. Here’s a chicken sent over from the Boar, here’s a tongue from the Boar, and here are one or two little things from the Boar which I hope you won’t disdain. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again almost as soon as he had sat, “see before me the very boy I used to play with in his happy childhood? And may I—may I—?”

By “May I,” he meant could he shake hands? I agreed, and he did so passionately, then sat down again.

“Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink our thanks to Fortune, and may she always choose her favorites with such good judgment! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, getting up again, “see someone before me—and drink to that someone too—without once more expressing—May I—may I—?”

I said he could, and he shook my hand again, drained his glass, and turned it upside down. I followed his example; and if I had turned myself upside down before drinking, the wine could hardly have gone more directly to my head.

Mr. Pumblechook served me the chicken’s liver wing and the finest slice of tongue—none of those inaccessible dead ends of pork now—and paid comparatively little attention to his own plate. “Ah! poultry, poultry! Little did you imagine,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the bird on the dish, “when you were a fledgling, what awaited you. Little did you think you’d provide refreshment under this humble roof for someone who—Call it a weakness, if you like,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “but may I? May I—?”

Repeating my permission was becoming unnecessary, so he immediately went ahead. How he managed it so often without injuring himself on my knife, I cannot tell.

“And your sister,” he continued, after eating steadily for a while, “who had the honor of raising you by hand! It’s a sad picture, to think she can no longer fully understand that honor. May—”

I saw that he was preparing to descend on me again and stopped him.

“We’ll drink to her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, reclining in his chair, quite limp with admiration, “that’s how you recognize them, sir!” (Who “sir” was I cannot say, but it certainly wasn’t me, and no third person was present.) “That’s how you recognize the noble-minded, sir!”

“By eight o’clock I had in fact reached a height of seventeen miles above the earth’s surface. It appeared plain to me, therefore, that my speed of ascent was increasing, and that some slight acceleration would have been perceptible even without my having thrown out the ballast. The pain in my head and ears came back violently from time to time, and my nose still occasionally bled; yet, taken altogether, my sufferings were considerably less than one might have anticipated. Breathing, however, grew more difficult with every moment, and each breath was accompanied by an annoying convulsive movement of the chest. I now took out the condensing apparatus and prepared it for instant use.

“The prospect of the earth at this stage of my ascent was truly lovely. To the west, north, and south, stretching as far as sight could reach, lay an unlimited expanse of seemingly placid ocean, whose blue grew deeper with each moment and which was already beginning to show a faint convexity. Far away to the east, though quite clearly distinguishable, stretched the islands of Great Britain, all the Atlantic shores of France and Spain, and a little of the northern African continent. No vestige of a single building was visible, and mankind’s most magnificent cities had vanished entirely from the earth’s face. From the rock of Gibraltar, diminished now to an indistinct speck, the dark Mediterranean extended eastward to the limit of my sight, sprinkled with bright islands as the heavens are sprinkled with stars. At last its whole volume of water appeared to plunge headlong into the gulf beyond the horizon, and I caught myself listening on tiptoe for the reverberations of that tremendous waterfall. Above me the sky was jet-black, and the stars shone with extraordinary brilliance.

“About this time the pigeons appeared to be suffering greatly, and I resolved to set them free. I first released one from its bonds, a handsome pigeon mottled with gray, and set him on the edge of the wicker basket. He seemed exceedingly distressed, glancing anxiously about, fluttering his wings, and cooing loudly, but nothing would induce him to venture away from the car. Finally I picked him up and tossed him some six yards clear of the balloon. Instead of trying to descend, as I had supposed he would, he struggled most violently to return, uttering cries of great shrillness and intensity as he did so. In the end he regained his previous perch on the rim; but scarcely had he reached it before his head sank against his breast and he dropped dead inside the car.”

I thought this curious lie had been told with wonderful simplicity and grace. But I had only heard it once, and that makes a difference. No doubt the others had enjoyed it when it was new.

Sir Dinadan the Humorist woke first and soon roused everyone else with a rather feeble practical joke. He tied several metal mugs to a dog’s tail and let him loose. The terrified animal raced around the room, with all the other dogs barking after him. They slammed into everything in their path, creating complete confusion and a deafening racket. Every man and woman in the crowd laughed until tears ran down their faces, and some fell out of their chairs and rolled on the floor in delight. They were just like a crowd of children. Sir Dinadan was so proud of what he had done that he kept explaining, over and over until it became tiresome, how this immortal idea had come to him. Like other humorists of his kind, he was still laughing after everyone else had finished. His success pleased him so much that he decided to give a speech—a funny speech, naturally. I don’t think I had ever heard so many exhausted old jokes strung together. He was worse than the minstrels, worse than a circus clown. It seemed especially sad to be sitting here, thirteen hundred years before my birth, hearing the same dull, decaying jokes that had made my stomach ache when I was a boy thirteen hundred years later. It almost persuaded me that a new joke was impossible. Everyone laughed at these ancient things—but people always do; I had noticed that centuries afterward. Of course, the mocker didn’t laugh—I mean the boy. No, he sneered; there was nothing he wouldn’t sneer at. He said most of Sir Dinadan’s jokes were rotten, and the rest had turned to stone. I liked that idea, since I thought myself that geological periods were the only proper way to measure the majestic age of some of those jokes. But this clever observation meant nothing to the boy, because geology hadn’t been invented yet. Still, I wrote the remark down and planned, if I survived, to educate the country until it could appreciate it. There is no sense in throwing away something good simply because the public isn’t ready for it.

Now Sir Kay got up and began stoking the machinery of his storytelling, using me as fuel.
